identity.title: Stimulant/substance exposure: caffeine, energy drinks, decongestants, beta-agonists, cocaine/amphetamines, alcohol binge (holiday heart), recent withdrawal

technique.how: Ask non-judgementally about the 24-48 h before the palpitations: caffeine/energy drinks (amount), decongestants, inhaled or oral beta-agonists, thyroid hormone, cocaine/amphetamines/MDMA, cannabis, nicotine, and alcohol quantity (binge in the preceding day or two) or abrupt cessation of alcohol/benzodiazepines; ask about weight-loss or 'pre-workout' supplements.
technique.prerequisites: Privacy and, when relevant, a urine drug screen or ethanol level to corroborate; check the pulse or rhythm strip during symptoms if ongoing.

interpretation.positive_finding: A temporal link to a stimulant, sympathomimetic or alcohol binge supports sinus tachycardia, ectopy or 'holiday heart' AF as the mechanism, and in cocaine/amphetamine use raises ischaemia and ventricular arrhythmia risk.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of exposures removes a reversible trigger but does not lower the probability of a primary arrhythmia; documented symptom-rhythm correlation is still required in recurrent palpitations.
interpretation.pitfalls: Attributing palpitations to caffeine or anxiety without a rhythm strip misses AF and SVT (cardiac cause in 43% of 190 consecutive palpitations patients, Weber 1996 Abstract); patients under-report alcohol and illicit drugs.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: ECG, electrolytes and rhythm capture, then trigger withdrawal with follow-up; negative: proceed to ambulatory monitoring based on symptom pattern, not to reassurance.

sources.citation: Weber BE, Kapoor WN. Evaluation and outcomes of patients with palpitations. Am J Med 1996;100:138-148.
Thavendiranathan P, Bagai A, Khoo C, Dorian P, Choudhry NK. Does this patient with palpitations have a cardiac arrhythmia? JAMA 2009;302:2135-2143.
Ettinger PO, Wu CF, De La Cruz C, Weisse AB, Ahmed SS, Regan TJ. Arrhythmias and the "Holiday Heart": alcohol-associated cardiac rhythm disorders. Am Heart J 1978;95:555-562.
Zimetbaum P, Josephson ME. Evaluation of patients with palpitations. N Engl J Med 1998;338:1369-1373.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use a stimulant history to explain palpitations with syncope, chest pain, known structural heart disease or an abnormal ECG.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Cocaine/amphetamine-associated palpitations with chest pain, hypertension or wide-complex rhythm require ACS and toxicology pathways; alcohol withdrawal with tachycardia needs withdrawal management.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Self-reported substance use is unreliable; no accuracy data for the history item.

extraction_notes: No diagnostic-accuracy data for stimulant, caffeine or alcohol exposure as a predictor of arrhythmia in patients with palpitations. The JAMA RCE (Thavendiranathan 2009, PMID 19920238, Abstract) lists LRs for cardiac-disease history (2.03), palpitations during sleep (2.29), at work (2.17), panic disorder (0.26) and duration <5 min (0.38) but no stimulant/alcohol item, and states 'No other features significantly alter the probability of clinically significant arrhythmia'. Weber 1996 (PMID 8629647, Abstract): etiology cardiac in 43%, psychiatric 31%, miscellaneous 10%, unknown 16% of 190 consecutive patients - background prevalence, not accuracy. Ettinger 1978 and Zimetbaum 1998 have no PubMed abstracts; cited for the holiday-heart concept and expert review only. Search 'caffeine consumption arrhythmia palpitations prospective' returned only a narrative review (PMID 29474816: coffee's effects on arrhythmias 'neutral').
